title: I gave it back
hook: never say "I lost it," say "I returned it" (Enchiridion 11)

segments.voice: Yesterday: what do I have for this? That was your line too. When something hard arrived, did you reach into the bag for one tool? Day three hundred forty-three, the end of a week.

Checking out of a hotel, nobody mourns the room. You slept well, you liked the view, you maybe stole the little soaps. Then you hand back the key card and walk out, and it doesn't feel like losing anything. It was never yours. You were a guest. Now notice how differently we talk about almost everything else. I lost my job. I lost my wallet. I lost my grandmother. Section eleven of the handbook takes aim at one small verb, and suggests trading it for another. Today: I gave it back.
screen: `HANDING BACK THE KEY CARD.` → `I LOST IT.` → `ONE SMALL VERB.`

segments.voice: First, the line. In George Long's translation: "Never say about anything, I have lost it; but say I have restored it." Restored in the old sense: given back, returned. Second, how far he takes it. Epictetus doesn't stop at wallets. Your child has died? It was given back. Your land was taken? That too was given back. It's one of the hardest passages in the handbook, and he doesn't soften it. Some readers find comfort there, a way of holding grief inside gratitude. Others feel it asks too much too soon. Both are honest responses, and nobody has to decide today. Third, the objection. Someone in the handbook protests: but the person who took my land is a crook. Epictetus answers: what does it matter to you which hand the giver used to ask for it back? It's a hard reply, and an interesting one. It moves attention from the thief to the gift. Fourth, the inn. While it's given to you, he says, take care of it as something not your own, the way travelers treat an inn. Not carelessly. Travelers can love an inn. But they don't carve their name into the door. Neighbors know this turn of phrase. In the book of Job, after terrible news, Job says: "the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD." A different home, a different understanding of who gives, the same small verb. And a look back at this week: dogma, the horse, the captain, as it comes, the leg, the bag of tools, and today, the key card handed back.
screen: `NEVER SAY I HAVE LOST IT.` · `EVEN THE HARDEST LOSSES.` · `WHICH HAND ASKED FOR IT BACK?` · `CARE FOR IT LIKE AN INN.` · then, large: `I GAVE IT BACK.`

segments.voice: Think of one small loss from this year. Not the biggest. Something you can hold without breaking: a job, a friendship that faded, a phone, a place you moved away from. Say it the usual way first, inside: I lost it. Notice how that sits. Then try Epictetus' verb: I gave it back. Say it slowly. If it feels false, let it be false; just notice. If it brings a little thanks for having had it, stay with that. The bell holds the time.
I gave it back. Epictetus' trade of verbs: not I lost it, but I returned it, and while you have it, care for it like an inn. Today's word.
Your line: I gave it back. The next time you're about to say I lost it today, even about keys, try the other verb. Another week on the porch done. Day three hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism speak of a loss as something returned rather than lost, and try to care for what they have as a guest cares for an inn.

what a scholar hears: apedoka, I gave back, set against apolesa, I lost; the inn image recurs in the Stoics for life as a stay, not a possession.
